chapters.title: Chapter 5: Funding Gaps, Tax Outflows and Surplus Cash

lessons.title: Short-Term Funding Options: Cash Credit, Overdraft, Bill Discounting and Working Capital Loans

children.text: Chapters 2 and 3 were about needing less cash. This one is about funding what remains. Every business has a gap between paying and being paid, and the only real questions are what shape that gap has and which instrument matches it. Get the match right and funding is cheap and invisible. Get it wrong and a profitable company pays 24% for money it could have had at 11%, or worse, funds a fifteen-year machine with a facility repayable on demand.

body.text: Match the funding to the shape of the gap. Short gaps need revolving money, seasonal peaks need seasonal money, and long-term assets need long-term money. Almost every funding disaster is a maturity mismatch.

children.text: First, Identify the Shape of Your Gap
Before comparing products, work out which of these you actually have. Most businesses have two or three at once, and they need different answers.

cells: Permanent working capital
The base level of stock and receivables that never goes away
Cash credit or overdraft, plus own funds. Part of it should be funded by equity, not debt
Seasonal peak
Festive or harvest build-up for three or four months a year
Cash credit headroom, a seasonal enhancement, or a working capital demand loan for the period
Specific invoice or order
One large confirmed invoice from a creditworthy buyer
Bill discounting, TReDS, factoring, or an order-backed facility
Long-term asset
A machine, a building, a fit-out
Term loan, equipment finance or lease. Never a revolving working capital line

body.text: The most expensive mistake in Indian SME finance is funding capex from the cash credit limit because the money happens to be available. The machine takes seven years to pay back, the limit is repayable on demand and reviewed annually, and the day the bank reduces the limit the business has no way to repay it.

children.text: The Instruments, and What They Really Cost
Indicative rates for a reasonably run SME with security. Your actual pricing depends on rating, relationship, security and the cycle, so treat these as relative positions rather than quotes.

cells: Cash credit
Stock and receivables, with margin
About 9% to 13%
Everyday working capital. Interest only on what is drawn
Overdraft
Property, fixed deposit or other collateral
About 10% to 14%
Flexible buffer, especially when stock is hard to monitor
Working capital demand loan
Same security as cash credit
About 8.5% to 11%
A known amount for a known period, usually cheaper than cash credit
Bill or invoice discounting
The accepted invoice itself
About 8% to 12%
Turning one large confirmed invoice into cash now
TReDS
Buyer-accepted invoice, priced off the buyer
Often the cheapest available to an MSME seller
MSMEs supplying large corporates and PSUs
Unsecured business loan
Nothing, usually with a personal guarantee
About 16% to 24%
Speed when collateral is unavailable, for short periods only
Fintech or revenue-based finance
Future receipts
Often 18% and above, once fees are annualised
Bridging a genuine short gap, not funding a business model

body.text: Always annualise the fee, not just the rate. A facility quoting "2% for 60 days" is about 12% a year, but "2% processing plus 1.5% a month" is over 20%. Ask for the all-in annual cost including processing fees, renewal fees, unused limit charges and any minimum interest clause, then compare like with like.

body.title: Why cash credit is cheaper than it looks

children.text: Cash credit charges interest on the daily outstanding balance, not on the sanctioned limit. That single feature makes it far cheaper than an equivalent loan for a business whose needs fluctuate.
A ₹50 lakh limit, average utilisation ₹25 lakh, at 11%:
about ₹2.75 lakh of interest a year.
A ₹50 lakh term loan at 11%:
about ₹5.5 lakh of interest a year, drawn or not.
Add the facility costs:
a processing fee of around 0.5% of the limit is about ₹25,000 a year, plus renewal and documentation charges.

Two habits follow from this. First, sweep surplus cash into the cash credit account rather than a current account, because every day the balance sits there it reduces the interest charged. Second, do not treat a large sanctioned limit as free. Unused limits can attract commitment charges, and a permanently drawn limit tells the bank something you may not want it to conclude.

body.title: Cost of discounting one invoice
body.prompt: Konkan Ceramics discounts a ₹30 lakh invoice that is due in 45 days, at a discounting rate of 9.5% a year. Ignoring processing fees, what does that cost, in rupees? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹30,00,000 times 9.5% is ₹2,85,000 for a full year. For 45 days, multiply by 45 divided by 365, which gives about ₹35,137. That is roughly 1.2% of the invoice value to receive the money 45 days early. Compare it against what the cash does for you: if it lets you take a 3% early payment discount from a supplier, or avoid a stock-out, it is clearly worth it.

children.text: How the Bank Decides What You Can Draw
A cash credit limit is a ceiling, not an entitlement. What you may actually draw on any given day is the drawing power, calculated monthly from the stock statement you submit.

body.caption: Margins vary by bank and by asset, commonly around 25% on stock and 40% on receivables

children.text: For Konkan Ceramics, with ₹1.8 crore of stock, ₹1.2 crore of creditors and ₹2.4 crore of receivables, at a 25% margin on paid-for stock and 40% on receivables, drawing power works out to about ₹1.89 crore. Two consequences matter for cash management.
Stock bought on credit does not create drawing power.
Creditors are deducted first, precisely so the bank does not finance what the supplier is already financing.
Old receivables are usually excluded.
Most banks disallow invoices beyond 90 days, so the ageing problem from Lesson 3.1 quietly shrinks your borrowing capacity at the same time.
The stock statement is a real document.
Overstating stock to lift drawing power is fraud, and it is the single most common way SME banking relationships end badly.

body.text: Watch the health of the account, not just the balance. Under the RBI framework, borrower accounts are flagged as Special Mention Accounts when dues remain unpaid, SMA-0 up to 30 days, SMA-1 from 31 to 60 and SMA-2 from 61 to 90, with classification done as part of the day-end process, and an account generally becomes an NPA beyond 90 days. For a cash credit account, staying continuously over the limit or unable to service interest is what triggers it. Once an account is flagged, every other lender sees it.

body.title: What you can actually draw
body.textWithBlank: The amount a business may draw on its cash credit account on a given day is set by its ___ power, calculated from the monthly stock statement.
body.explanation: The sanctioned limit is the ceiling. Drawing power is the working number, and it falls when stock is bought on credit, when receivables age past the bank's cut-off, or when stock is written down. Many businesses discover their real limit only in the month they most need it.

children.text: Choosing, for a Real Gap

Konkan Ceramics' 13-week forecast from Lesson 4.2 showed a trough of about ₹43 lakh, lasting roughly three months through the festive build-up, after which collections repay it. Here is what funding that same gap costs by route.

body.title: Cost of funding a ₹43 lakh gap for three months (₹ thousand)

children.text: The cheapest route costs about ₹1.18 lakh and the most expensive about ₹3.01 lakh, for exactly the same cash, for exactly the same three months. The difference is not negotiation skill, it is preparation: the business that arranged a cash credit limit last year has the cheap option available, and the one that did not is choosing between expensive alternatives in the week it runs short.

body.title: What makes a bank say yes, and what makes it hesitate

columns.label: Strengthens your case
points: Audited financials filed on time and consistent with GST returns
A cash credit account that fluctuates, showing the business actually turns over
Stock statements submitted every month without reminders
Clean repayment record and a good commercial credit report
A cash forecast showing the peak need and how it reverses

columns.label: Raises questions
points: A limit that is fully drawn every single day of the year
Turnover in the account far below reported sales
Receivables ageing worsening while the limit request grows
Capex clearly funded from working capital limits
Related-party advances leaving the business while it asks for more

body.title: Which facility fits?
body.question: A components maker has confirmed orders from a large listed customer, invoices accepted on 75-day terms, and needs cash now to buy raw material for the next batch. It has a cash credit limit that is 90% drawn. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Take an unsecured business loan at 19% for twelve months
Discount the accepted invoices, or route them through TReDS if the buyer is on a platform
Ask the promoter to bring in personal funds as an unsecured loan
Delay supplier payments by 30 days to self-fund the batch
body.explanation: The business has exactly the asset that invoice financing is designed for: accepted invoices from a creditworthy buyer. Discounting or TReDS prices off that buyer, costs a fraction of unsecured borrowing, and self-liquidates when the buyer pays. An unsecured loan funds a 75-day gap with twelve-month money, promoter funds should be reserved for genuine equity needs, and stretching suppliers brings the consequences from Lesson 3.2.

body.title: The limit is fully drawn and the bank wants a plan
body.scenario: Konkan Ceramics has a ₹50 lakh cash credit limit that has been drawn at 48 to 50 lakh every day for nine months. The relationship manager has asked for a meeting before the annual renewal. Sales are growing, receivables are ageing, a ₹15 lakh packing machine was bought from the limit last year, and the promoter wants to ask for an enhancement to ₹75 lakh.
body.prompt: How do you prepare for that meeting, and what do you actually ask for?
body.modelAnswer:
Understand what the bank is seeing before you walk in.
1. A permanently drawn limit is not working capital behaviour, it is a term loan in disguise. The bank knows it, and the machine purchase confirms it.
2. Ageing receivables reduce drawing power, so the gap between sanctioned limit and eligible drawing power is probably already narrow. Check it before the meeting, not during.
Prepare the case with numbers, not adjectives.
3. Bring the 13-week forecast and the annual bridge from Lesson 4.1, showing the peak need, the month it occurs and the month it reverses. A bank funds a peak it can see, not a general shortage.
4. Show the working capital improvement plan from Lesson 2.2: receivable days from 73 to 60, inventory days from 78 to 65, releasing about ₹91 lakh. That plan reduces the enhancement you need and demonstrates control.
5. Own the machine mistake openly and propose the fix: carve out ₹15 lakh into a term loan over five years, which restores the revolving nature of the limit and matches the asset's life.
Then make a specific, structured request.
6. Ask for an enhancement to a defined number supported by the forecast, not a round figure, and be ready to explain the drawing power arithmetic behind it.
7. Ask for a seasonal sub-limit for the festive quarter rather than a permanently higher limit, which is often easier to sanction and cheaper overall.
8. Offer to route accepted invoices from the largest dealers through bill discounting, which reduces pressure on the limit and gives the bank self-liquidating exposure.
9. Commit to monthly stock statements and quarterly ageing reports, and then actually send them.
What to avoid saying.
10. Do not present growth as the reason for the request without showing the cash arithmetic. Every borrower says sales are growing. The ones who get sanctioned show why growth consumes cash and when it gives it back.

body.title: Review your funding structure this quarter
steps: List every facility: type, sanctioned limit, current outstanding, rate, security and renewal date.
Calculate the all-in annual cost of each, including processing, renewal and unused limit charges.
Check whether any long-term asset has been funded from a short-term facility, and plan to refinance it.
Compare your current drawing power against the sanctioned limit, and find out which receivables the bank disallows.
Look at the cash credit balance over the last twelve months: does it fluctuate, or is it permanently drawn?
Identify which invoices are eligible for discounting or TReDS, and what that would cost against your cash credit rate.
Map your forecast peak need from Lesson 4.2 against total available headroom, and note the shortfall if any.
Diarise renewal dates 60 days in advance, because renewals negotiated under time pressure are expensive.

cards.definition: A revolving limit secured against stock and receivables, with interest charged on the daily outstanding.
What you may actually draw today, computed from stock and eligible receivables after margins.
The share of an asset's value the bank will not lend against, commonly 25% on stock and 40% on receivables.
A fixed amount for a fixed period against the same security, usually priced below cash credit.
Receiving cash now against an accepted invoice, for a discount charge based on the days saved.
Funding a long-lived asset with short-term money. The most common cause of avoidable business failure.

points: Identify the shape of the gap first: permanent, seasonal, invoice-specific or long-term. The shape chooses the instrument.
Never fund capex from a working capital limit. It is repayable on demand and reviewed every year.
Cash credit charges interest only on what is drawn, so ₹25 lakh of average use on a ₹50 lakh limit costs about ₹2.75 lakh a year.
Annualise every fee before comparing. The same ₹43 lakh gap for three months costs about ₹1.18 lakh on cash credit and about ₹3.01 lakh from a fintech lender.
Drawing power, not the sanctioned limit, decides what you can draw, and ageing receivables quietly reduce it.
A permanently drawn limit signals to the bank that the facility has become a term loan. Fix the structure before the renewal meeting.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional. All rates, margins and fees are indicative illustrations for teaching, not quotes, and actual pricing depends on the borrower, security and market conditions. Regulatory classification norms are summarised and can change. Confirm current terms with your bank and your chartered accountant.
